body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals, specifically the conversion of lead into gold, is subject to strict reporting thresholds to prevent the destabilization of the regional currency. Under the Autumnwood Accords, lead remains lead for tax and regulatory purposes until a formal assay by the Guild's Assay Desk confirms the permanence and purity of the transmutation. Any gold produced via transmutation must be declared to the Guild within twenty-four hours of the conversion. This ensures that the influx of "new" gold does not lead to hyper-inflation or the corruption of the market.

Mages who engage in large-scale transmutation for the purpose of flooding the market with gold are subject to heavy fines and may be required to contribute a portion of their yield to the Guild's treasury. The Innovators may argue that this stifles the progress of alchemical science, but the Conservators maintain that economic stability is a prerequisite for magical safety. For inquiries regarding the identification of fees for these assays, see § 900.4. For the reporting of these material enchantments, see § 900.2.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The use of polymorph magic to alter the shape of coinage is strictly forbidden. The Guild maintains that the shape of a coin is not its denomination; a gold coin shaped like a dragon is still a gold coin, but a copper coin shaped like a gold coin is a criminal offense. Any attempt to use polymorph magic to deceive a merchant or a citizen regarding the denomination of a currency is a direct violation of the Accords. Such acts are considered a form of high-level fraud and will be met with immediate seizure of all the offender's current currency.

Furthermore, the use of polymorph magic to create "counterfeit" coins—those that possess the correct shape but lack the required magical signature of the Guild-approved mint—is a capital offense within the Guild's jurisdiction. The Aegis Magi are authorized to use "Truth-Sensing" wards in all major marketplaces to detect such discrepancies. For the reporting of these material enchantments, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees for legitimate minting, see § 900.4.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
A lien is a legal claim on an asset; the fact that a lien is hidden from public view does not negate its existence. Furthermore, any attempt to use invisibility magic or "veiling" spells to hide a lien on a traded object is a violation of the Accords. An invisible lien is still a lien, and an attempt to conceal it is a deliberate act of fraud. All liens must be recorded in a visible, legible manner on the item's title or accompanying documentation. Any merchant who attempts to sell an item with a concealed lien shall be prosecuted for fraud.

If a lien is discovered to have been hidden using active magic, the offending mage shall be subject to the Paradox Trial as outlined in § 800.2. The Guild maintains that transparency in debt is essential for the health of the Midlands' economy. For the reporting of the enchantments used to veil such liens, see § 900.2. For the legal consequences of providing false provenance regarding an item's debt status, see § 900.5.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The use of a "Wish" or any high-level reality-warping spell to alter, erase, or rewrite a filed magical return or a notarized contract is strictly prohibited. A wish does not rewrite the stamp of the Accords Desk. Once a document has been filed and stamped by an authorized clerk, it is considered a permanent record of the Guild. Any attempt to use reality-warping magic to retroactively change the terms of a contract or the amount of a reported enchantment is a violation of the fundamental stability of the Accord.

Mages who attempt such actions are viewed as threats to the very fabric of the Guild's legal framework and will be subject to the most severe sanctions, including a permanent Seal of Silence or a Paradox Trial. The Guild's records are protected by high-level "Stasis Wards" to prevent such tampering. For the procedures regarding the Paradox Trial, see § 800.2. For the reporting of material enchantments that might be used to attempt such rewrites, see § 900.2.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The Guild does not recognize the "Wario Coin" as a legal tender or a valid form of currency within the Midlands. The Wario Coin is classified as a private tender and carries no weight in Guild-governed transactions. Any merchant who accepts Wario Coins as payment for Guild-regulated goods or services is doing so at their own risk and is not entitled to Guild protection or mediation in the event of a dispute. Furthermore, the Guild will not facilitate the exchange of Wario Coins for any recognized currency.

Any attempt to force the Guild to recognize the Wario Coin as a standard currency is a violation of the Accords. The Aegis Magi are instructed to ignore any requests for currency conversion involving this token. For matters regarding the identification of fees for legitimate currency exchange, see § 900.4. For the reporting of material enchantments that might be used to fake Wario Coins, see § 900.2.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
Any storage vessel, including but not limited to a Bag of Holding, used to conceal assets from the Guild's oversight is considered an "off-books" vault. However, the Accords Desk maintains that "off-books" is still "books" if a clerk can smell it. The use of extra-dimensional storage to hide wealth from taxation, reporting, or seizure is a violation of the Guild's right to oversee the flow of magical assets. Any such vessel discovered in the possession of a Guild member that contains undeclared assets will be subject to immediate audit.

The Guild reserves the right to inspect any such storage vessels during a formal audit or if there is reasonable suspicion of fraud. The owner of the vessel must provide a full manifest of its contents. For the reporting of material enchantments that facilitate such storage, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees associated with the registration of large-scale storage vessels, see § 900.4.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
Any transaction involving a "bound object"—an item that possesses the ability to move, act, or defend itself independently—is subject to heightened scrutiny. Because such objects can "walk away" from their owners or act as autonomous agents, they are considered high-risk collateral. Any contract involving a bound object as collateral must include a "Binding Clause" that prevents the object from fleeing its owner or the lender during a dispute. Failure to secure a bound object properly during a transaction is the sole responsibility of the seller.

If a bound object leaves its owner's possession during a trade due to a lack of proper binding, the seller shall be held liable for the full value of the item. The Aegis Magi may be called upon to "tether" such objects during high-value negotiations. For the reporting of the enchantments used to bind such objects, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees for the notarization of binding clauses, see § 900.4.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
Any series of transfigurations, enchantments, or physical alterations that are so complex that a reasonable toad would be confused are to be read as a single scheme. The Guild does not recognize "layered" deception where a mage uses multiple minor transfigurations to hide a major illegal one. If the cumulative effect of several minor magical changes is to obscure the true nature of an object, it shall be treated as a single act of fraud. This prevents mages from bypassing the laws of the Accords by breaking down a large violation into several smaller, "permissible" ones.

The Aegis Magi are instructed to look for the "intent of the weave" rather than the individual threads of the spell. If the ultimate result of a magical process is a violation of the Accords, the entire process is subject to sanction. For the reporting of complex material enchantments, see § 900.2. For the identification of fees for auditing complex magical schemes, see § 900.4.

sections.title: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets
sections.brief: Named classes. Quiet List stays quiet.

body.heading: Prohibited Spells in Financial Markets
body.text:
Any mage, Innovator, or Conservator engaged in the facilitation of commerce, the brokering of arcane assets, or the management of guild-sanctioned vaults shall be strictly prohibited from employing specific classes of spells designed to bypass the cognitive faculties of a counterparty. Under the Autumnwood Accords, the use of high-level charms of compulsion, charms of suggestion, or any transmutation intended to alter the perceived weight or value of a physical asset during a transaction is strictly forbidden. Such actions constitute a primary violation of the Accords and shall be subject to immediate referral to the Aegis Magi for investigation. Furthermore, any spell that induces a state of "magical euphoria" or "docile compliance" in a potential buyer or seller is classified as a predatory arcane act.

The Guild maintains a strict prohibition on the use of "Veil-Shifting" and "Memory-Softening" magic within any marketplace, whether physical or ethereal. While the Innovators may argue for the utility of such magic in "market smoothing," the Conservators maintain that the sanctity of the buyer's will is the bedrock of the Midlands' economic stability. Any mage found utilizing these classes of magic in a financial context shall be subject to the Paradox Trial as outlined in § 800.2. The penalties for such violations may range from the permanent sealing of the offending mage's casting ability to a term of service in a pocket-prison, depending on the scale of the financial discrepancy caused.

Furthermore, no mage may use "True Sight" or "Identify" as a means of coercion to force a sale. While these spells are standard tools of the trade, their use to strip a seller of their "right to privacy regarding arcane secrets" is a violation of the Accords. The Guild recognizes the distinction between a professional assay and a predatory search. Any merchant who refuses to allow a standard, non-invasive assay by a licensed clerk may do so, but any mage who attempts to bypass this refusal using invasive scrying or piercing magic shall be fined. See § 1001.1 for the general definition of fraud.

The Quiet List shall remain strictly confidential and is not to be referenced in any public catalog, ledger, or marketplace declaration. No mage shall recite the names of items or methods contained within the Quiet List in any tavern, public square, or marketplace. Any breach of this secrecy by a mage, even if the breach is not intended for financial gain, shall be considered a felony under the Accords. The secrecy of the Quiet List is paramount to the safety of the Midlands; thus, any mage who discusses "Quiet items" in a commercial setting shall face immediate sanctions. See § 300.3 for the procedure of listing such items without public notice.

sections.title: Valuation After Alteration
sections.brief: Who assays. Petrified inventory is still inventory.

body.heading: Valuation After Alteration
body.text:
Any magical asset, artifact, or mundane item subjected to transfiguration, transmutation, or any other form of structural alteration by a licensed practitioner shall be subject to a mandatory re-valuation before it may be entered into the Guild’s ledger of commerce. The primary burden of initiating this assessment lies with the caster of the alteration; should the change be performed for a third party, the contracting party shall be held liable for the costs of the assay. The Accords Desk maintains that a change in physical state—be it the hardening of flesh into stone, the sharpening of iron into glass, or the expansion of volume—constitutes a fundamental shift in the object’s utility and marketability.

The official assay shall be conducted by a Guild-sanctioned Appraiser of the Fourth Circle or higher. No private valuation, regardless of the complexity of the arcane mathematics employed by the practitioner, shall be recognized by the Accords Desk as a final determination of value for the purposes of taxation or trade. This requirement applies to all items moving through the Midlands markets under the jurisdiction of Archmage Veyra. If a practitioner fails to submit an object for assay following a significant alteration, they shall be held in breach of the Accords, and any subsequent sale of said object may be voided by the Aegis Magi.

Furthermore, the Accords Desk explicitly clarifies that "Petrified Inventory is still Inventory." The transition of an object into a petrified, fossilized, or otherwise inert mineral state does not exempt the owner from their existing storage fees or their obligation to report the item’s existence. While the market value may be severely diminished by petrification, the legal status of the item as a piece of property remains unchanged. See § 1001.3 for further clarification on the persistence of property rights during state-change events.

body.heading: Illusion-Based Fraud
body.text:
The use of illusion magic to distort the perceived reality of a commercial transaction is strictly prohibited under the Autumnwood Accords. This prohibition encompasses, but is not limited to, the creation of an illusion of goods, the distortion of the perceived price, or the fabrication of a phantom buyer. Any practitioner who utilizes *Major Image*, *Hallucinatory Terrain*, or any derivative school of deceptive weaving to induce a sale is subject to immediate seizure of their arcane focus and a referral to the Paradox Trial for the determination of appropriate sanctions.

Specifically, the creation of "Ghost Stock"—where an item appears to be present in a warehouse or storefront but is actually absent—is classified as a high-tier offense of the Accords. Similarly, any attempt to manipulate the perceived scarcity of a resource via atmospheric illusions shall be met with heavy fines and a potential revocation of the practitioner's license to operate within the Midlands. The Accords Desk does not distinguish between "artistic" illusion and "commercial" illusion when the latter results in a transfer of currency or goods; if the buyer’s consent was predicated on a falsehood of the senses, the transaction is null.

The fabrication of a buyer is considered a felony of the highest order within the Guild’s jurisdiction. This includes the use of simulacra or illusions to create a false sense of demand, thereby inflating the value of the seller's goods or creating a fraudulent market history. Practitioners found guilty of such acts shall be barred from all Guild-sanctioned markets for a period of no less than ten years. See § 700.4 regarding the limitations of simulacrum testimony in these matters.

body.heading: Material Alteration of Traded Goods
body.text:
Any practitioner intending to sell a good that has undergone material alteration must provide a comprehensive disclosure of the changes made. This disclosure must be explicit and must be presented in a manner that ensures the buyer is fully aware of the item's history. The burden of proof rests entirely upon the seller to demonstrate that the transfiguration was performed within the safety margins established by the Conservators. If an object has been aggregated—such as the fusing of multiple smaller items into a single larger entity—this must be documented as a primary structural change.

Permissible transfiguration is defined as any change that does not fundamentally alter the "Soul-Signature" of the item, as defined by the Conservators. If a transfiguration results in a permanent change to the item's weight, durability, or magical conductivity, a formal disclosure must be filed with the Accords Desk. Failure to disclose such alterations constitutes a breach of the Goodstyle Artisan standards and may lead to a permanent ban from the Guild's trade circles.

Historical annotations regarding these regulations can be found in C.C.D. 6125, 7355, and 10155. These records detail the evolution of "Permissible Transfiguration" from the early days of the Accords to the current tensions between the Innovators and the Conservators. Practitioners are advised that the Aegis Magi may conduct random inspections of high-value inventory to ensure compliance with these disclosure requirements. See § 400.4 for related specimen custody rules.

body.heading: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
body.text:
A magical asset provided as a gift or an endowment is subject to the same regulatory scrutiny as a standard sale, provided the asset possesses the capacity for autonomous action or delayed activation. Specifically, any item that "later bills the wearer" or imposes a recurring cost, fee, or obligation upon its owner after the initial transfer of possession shall be legally classified as an "Endowment of Magical Assets." This classification ensures that "gifts" cannot be used as a loophole to bypass the disclosure of hidden magical liens or recurring costs.

When an item is gifted, the donor must provide a "Certificate of Clean Title," certifying that no hidden geases, parasitic enchantments, or delayed-activation fees are attached to the object. If an item is discovered to have a hidden billing mechanism—such as a sentient hat that demands a monthly tribute of mana or gold—the original donor remains liable for the initial violation of the Accords. The recipient may seek a refund of the "gift" value, and the donor shall be subject to a fine for fraudulent endowment.

The Accords Desk recognizes that many magical items are inherently complex. However, the intent of the law is to prevent the "Trojan Horse" method of magical commerce. If an item possesses a "contractual" nature—where it performs a service in exchange for a resource—it must be declared as such at the moment of transfer. This prevents the circumvention of the § 600.3 prohibitions on unconscionable geases. See § 600.3 for details on geas as an unconscionable term.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
All commercial interactions involving magical goods must be predicated upon full and accurate disclosure. The seller is required to provide a comprehensive breakdown of the object's composition, its current market value, and the inherent risks associated with its use. A critical component of this requirement is the language of disclosure; the Accords Desk rules that information provided in a language the buyer does not speak or understand is not considered "full." If a practitioner sells a volatile artifact to a layperson using only high-arcane cantrips for description, the practitioner is liable for any subsequent accidents or malfunctions.

The "Risk" component of the disclosure must include a warning of any known "volatile" traits, such as a tendency to teleport, a high chance of mana-drain, or a history of unpredictable behavior. For items of significant power, a "Safety Briefing" must be provided, and the buyer must sign a waiver acknowledging the risks. This is particularly important for goods sourced from the frontiers of the Midlands, where the stability of magic is less certain.

The Accords Desk maintains that transparency is the foundation of the Autumnwood Accords. By ensuring that buyers are fully informed, the Guild minimizes the frequency of disputes that lead to the Paradox Trial. Failure to provide a clear, linguistically accessible disclosure is grounds for immediate seizure of the goods and a penalty from the Aegis Magi. See § 800.1 for the range of sanctions available for such non-compliance.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious metals is strictly regulated to prevent the destabilization of the regional economy. Under the Accords, lead remains lead for the purposes of taxation and trade reporting until such a time as the official Assay Desk agrees to certify the transmutation. A practitioner who creates gold through alchemy or spellcraft must submit their "Batch of Transmutation" to the Assay Desk for a formal verification of the metal's purity and origin.

Until the Assay Desk provides a "Certificate of Authenticity," any gold produced by a practitioner is considered "Uncertified Bullion" and may not be traded in public markets. Selling uncertified bullion as "Pure Gold" is a violation of the Accords and is punishable by a heavy fine and the temporary suspension of the practitioner's transmutation license. This rule exists to prevent the flooding of the market with magically-generated wealth, which would devalue the efforts of the Goodstyle Artisans and other legitimate producers.

The reporting threshold for transmutation is set at five ounces of precious metal. Any transmutation resulting in a yield below this amount is considered "Minor Transmutation" and does not require a formal Assay Desk filing, provided it is for personal use and not for resale. However, any sale of such "Minor" gold still requires a basic practitioner's license. See § 500.1 for rules on field casting for value.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The physical shape of a currency unit does not determine its denomination. The Accords Desk explicitly forbids the use of *Polymorph* or any other shape-shifting magic to alter the appearance of coins, notes, or other tender. A coin that has been magically altered to resemble a larger denomination is considered a fraudulent counterfeit. This includes "Shape-Shifting Tender," where a coin may change its appearance depending on the light or the viewer's perspective.

The Guild's position is that the "Essence of Value" is tied to the magical signature and weight of the currency, not its visual representation. If a practitioner attempts to pass a copper coin that has been visually altered to look like a gold sovereign, they shall be prosecuted for fraud. This rule is designed to prevent the confusion of common merchants and to maintain the integrity of the Midlands' trade networks.

Furthermore, the use of polymorph magic on currency is seen as a frivolous waste of arcane energy and a direct insult to the stability sought by the Conservators. Practitioners found engaging in such activities may be ordered to undergo a period of "Arcane Probation," during which their ability to cast non-combat spells is restricted. See § 1001.1 for general financial fraud rules.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
A hidden lien is still a lien. The Accords Desk establishes that any magical lien, debt, or claim placed upon a magical asset is legally binding, regardless of whether it is visually or magically concealed. An "Invisible Lien"—one that is hidden via *Invisibility*, *Masking*, or other concealment charms—is a direct violation of the Accords. All liens must be registered in a public ledger or at least disclosed to any potential buyer of the asset.

The purpose of this rule is to ensure that property rights are transparent. If a practitioner sells an item that is subject to a hidden lien, they are liable for the debt and any legal repercussions that arise from the debt's enforcement. The Aegis Magi are authorized to "Reveal All" on any high-value transaction, using detection spells to uncover any hidden magical signatures of ownership or debt.

A lien is defined as any magical binding that prevents the current holder of an item from fully utilizing its properties or selling it without the consent of a third party. If such a binding exists, it must be declared as a "Restrictive Covenant" in the sale contract. Failure to do so is considered a deliberate act of deception. See § 700.1 for evidence generally.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The use of a *Wish* or any other high-level reality-warping spell to rewrite, alter, or erase a filed tax return or a Guild registration is strictly prohibited. A *Wish* does not rewrite the stamp; the administrative record of the Accords Desk is considered a "Fixed Point of Bureaucracy." Any attempt to use reality-warping magic to retroactively change a past legal filing is a grave offense against the stability of the Guild's records.

The Accords Desk maintains that while magic can alter the world, it cannot overwrite the bureaucratic truth of the Guild. If a practitioner makes an error on a filed return, they must file an "Amendment of Record" through the standard channels. Attempting to "wish" the error out of existence is viewed as an act of magical insurrection and may be prosecuted as an attempt to subvert the sovereignty of Archmage Veyra.

Practitioners who attempt to use *Wish* for administrative purposes shall be subject to immediate impoundment of their magical focus. The Guild views the preservation of its records as a primary duty of the Conservators, and any magic that threatens the integrity of these records is treated with the utmost severity. See § 800.2 for Paradox Trial procedures.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The "Wario Coin" is not recognized as legal tender by the Mages' Guild or any other authority within the Autumnwood Accords. It is classified as "Private Tender" and may only be used in transactions between private parties who explicitly agree to its acceptance. The Guild does not provide any guarantees for its value, and it cannot be used to pay Guild fees, taxes, or fines.

Furthermore, the Guild notes that the "Wario Coin" holds even less value than common copper in many regional markets. Practitioners are advised that attempting to use Wario Coins for the purchase of restricted research materials or the settlement of debts with the Aegis Magi will result in the transaction being rejected without prejudice. The Guild does not wish to be associated with the "Wario Method" of commerce.

While the Guild does not actively ban the possession of Wario Coins, it refuses to provide any protections for those who trade in them. If a merchant accepts a Wario Coin and later finds it to be worthless, the Guild will not intervene. See § 1001.1 for general financial fraud and manipulation.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
Any storage vessel that expands the internal volume of an object—specifically the "Bag of Holding" and its variants—cannot be used as an "Off-Books Vault" to circumvent storage fees. The Accords Desk maintains that "Off-books is still books if a clerk can smell it." If a practitioner stores items in a Bag of Holding within the Midlands, those items are still subject to the Guild's inventory taxes and safety regulations.

The reasoning is based on the "Presence of Utility." If a practitioner uses a Bag of Holding to store goods for the purpose of trade or long-term storage, those goods are considered to be "in residence" within the Guild's jurisdiction. The use of such bags to hide inventory from the tax assessors is a violation of the Accords and will be treated as tax evasion.

The Aegis Magi are authorized to use "Sense Volume" spells to detect the contents of such bags during routine inspections. If a practitioner is found to be hiding a significant amount of inventory in a Bag of Holding to avoid the "Storage Fee," they will be assessed the back taxes plus a penalty for "Bureaucratic Evasion." See § 900.3 for record retention.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
The Guild recognizes that many magical items are "Bound"—meaning they possess a degree of autonomy or are tied to a specific caster. Any transaction involving a bound object is considered a "Secured Transaction" and requires a "Release of Bond" certificate. Collateral that can walk away, fly away, or otherwise act independently of its owner's will is subject to special restrictions.

If an item is used as collateral for a loan and it possesses the ability to move independently, the lender must place a "Geas of Stasis" on the object until the debt is satisfied. Failure to do so, or the attempt to sell a bound object without the consent of its "Master" (if one exists), is a violation of the Accords. The Guild seeks to prevent the "losing" of collateral due to the item's own agency.

In cases where an object's autonomy is so great that it cannot be reliably bound, it must be sold with a "Warning of Independent Agency." The buyer must acknowledge that the item may act against their interests and that the Guild provides no recourse for such actions. See § 600.3 for geas as an unconscionable term.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
When a practitioner performs a series of transfigurations on a single object—a "Layered Transfiguration Scheme"—the entire sequence shall be read as one single scheme for the purposes of appraisal and disclosure. If a sequence of changes is so complex that a "reasonable toad would be confused" by the final result compared to the original state, the practitioner must provide a full history of every step taken.

This prevents "incremental fraud," where a practitioner makes several small, seemingly insignificant changes to an object until it becomes something entirely different, thereby avoiding the reporting requirements of a major transfiguration. For the purposes of the Accords Desk, if the final product is unrecognizable from the original, it is a "Major Alteration" and requires a full Assay Desk certification.

The burden of disclosure is on the practitioner to provide a "Transmutation Map" for any item that has undergone more than three distinct material changes. This map must be filed with the Accords Desk before the item can be sold or traded. Failure to provide a clear map for a complex scheme will result in the item being seized for "Unregulated Alteration." See § 1001.3 for valuation after alteration.

sections.title: Illusion-Based Fraud
sections.brief: Illusion of goods, of price, of a buyer.

body.heading: Illusion-Based Fraud
body.text:
Illusion of goods, of price, of a buyer.

Any act of commerce involving the use of illusion magic to distort the perception of the tangible, the fiscal, or the corporeal nature of a transaction shall be deemed a primary violation of the Autumnwood Accords. The Accords Desk maintains that the integrity of the marketplace relies upon a shared reality; therefore, any mage who utilizes glamours to project the existence of inventory that does not exist in the physical plane, or to mask the physical decay of a product, shall be subject to immediate seizure of assets. This includes, but is not limited to, the projection of "phantom stock" to lure buyers into entering into binding contracts for goods that have been destroyed, sold elsewhere, or never produced. Such actions constitute a breach of the sanctity of the Midlands trade routes and shall be prosecuted under the standard of deceptive practice.

Furthermore, the manipulation of perceived price is strictly prohibited. A mage may not cast illusions that alter the visual representation of a price tag, the perceived quantity of a bulk shipment, or the perceived quality of a gemstone or reagent. The Guild recognizes that while the aesthetic appeal of a product may be enhanced through minor, non-persistent enchantments, any illusion that obscures the actual cost or the true weight of the item constitutes fraud. The burden of proof in such cases shall rest upon the seller to provide a "True-Sight" verification at the time of the transaction, ensuring that the buyer is interacting with the reality of the offer.

The most severe category of illusion-based fraud involves the fabrication of the buyer. The use of illusions to create a "simulated clientele" to inflate the perceived popularity of a shop, or the use of illusions to impersonate a high-status individual to secure favorable credit terms, is a felony under Guild law. Any mage found to have manufactured a "crowd" to create a false sense of demand shall be fined three times the projected value of the fraud. See § 1001.1. Any merchant caught employing such tactics shall have their trading license revoked by the Accords Desk. The Guild maintains that while the Innovators may seek to push the boundaries of sensory manipulation, the marketplace is a zone of absolute transparency. Any ambiguity created by magical means that leads to a financial loss for a non-caster shall be rectified by the Guild’s oversight committee, with the offending mage bearing all costs of restitution.

sections.title: Material Alteration of Traded Goods
sections.brief: MATCH THE FILED PHOTO: aggregation; permissible transfiguration; disclosure; burden; cross-refs; historical annotations C.C.D. 6125 / 7355 / 10155.

body.heading: Material Alteration of Traded Goods
body.text:
Any merchant, artisan, or mage-trader engaged in the commerce of enchanted, mundane, or semi-sentient goods shall be held strictly liable for the material alteration of such items following the point of sale. Under the Autumnwood Accords, the integrity of a trade is predicated upon the physical and metaphysical state of the object at the moment of exchange. An "alteration" is defined as any change to the object’s primary form, weight, utility, or inherent magical properties that occurs without the express written consent of the purchaser. This includes, but is not limited to, the expansion of a container’s interior volume, the modification of a weapon’s reach, or the transmutation of a material’s base essence. See § 1001.3 regarding valuation after such alterations.

The burden of proof regarding the original state of a traded good rests upon the seller. If a dispute arises concerning the degradation or transformation of a product, the seller must provide a certified "State of Origin" manifest. In cases where the item is an enchanted artifact, the seller shall provide a recorded magical signature to accompany the physical description. If a buyer can demonstrate that an item has undergone an unauthorized aggregation—such as the merging of two distinct magical artifacts into a single, unstable composite—the seller shall be liable for the full restitution of the purchase price plus a punitive fee of twenty percent of the original value. Furthermore, any permissible transfiguration must be disclosed as a primary feature of the item; if a transfiguration is hidden or triggered by a mechanism not revealed at the time of sale, it shall be deemed a fraudulent alteration.

All transactions involving complex transfigurations must be cross-referenced with the established precedents for material stability. For instance, if an item undergoes a change that results in a net increase of mass or volume without a corresponding increase in utility, it shall be flagged for inspection by the Aegis Magi. Historical annotations regarding the stability of such items may be found in C.C.D. 6125, 7355, and 10155. Any seller found to have intentionally obscured the "Material Alteration" status of a good through layered enchantments shall face a Paradox Trial for deceptive practice. See § 800.2 for the procedure of such a trial.

body.heading: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
body.text:
Any magical asset, artifact, or enchanted garment bestowed upon a recipient as a gift or endowment shall be subject to the Accords' regulations regarding "Deferred Consideration." A common point of litigation arises when a gift—such as a ceremonial hat, cloak, or staff—is found to possess a "billing" enchantment or a parasitic mana-drain mechanism that activates after a period of possession. For the purposes of the Autumnwood Accords, such an item is not a true gift but an unconscionable endowment. If a gift later bills the wearer, the recipient is entitled to a full dissolution of the debt and the immediate seizure of the item by the Guild’s enforcement agents.

The distinction between a "Gift" and an "Endowment" rests on the intent of the donor and the presence of a latent obligation. A gift is a complete transfer of ownership with no strings attached. An endowment is a transfer of use that carries a hidden, delayed, or recurring cost, whether that cost be in gold, mana, blood, or service. Mages who provide "free" magical items to the public or to fellow mages are cautioned that any latent mechanism designed to extract value from the user post-possession shall be treated as a violation of the Accords. Such items must be registered with the Accords Desk as "Conditional Endowments" before they may be distributed.

Furthermore, if an endowment is discovered to be predatory—meaning the cost of the "gift" exceeds the market value of the item by a factor of three or more—the donor shall be subject to a mandatory audit by the Conservators. Archmage Theron has decreed that the stability of the Midlands' economy relies on the clarity of these transfers. If a donor attempts to bypass these rules by claiming the billing mechanism is a "protective ward" or a "training exercise," the burden of proof remains on the donor to demonstrate that the cost is non-exploitative. See § 600.3 for related prohibitions on unconscionable terms in magical contracts.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
The principle of Full and Accurate Disclosure is the cornerstone of all commercial arcane transactions. Every seller of magical goods is mandated to provide a comprehensive disclosure of an item’s composition, its appraised value, and its inherent risks. This disclosure must be presented in a manner that is accessible to the buyer. It is a specific violation of the Accords to provide a disclosure that is technically accurate but practically obscured. For example, providing a description of a volatile explosive in a language the buyer does not speak, or using overly dense arcane jargon to hide a catastrophic failure rate, shall be deemed a failure of disclosure.

Full disclosure requires three distinct components. First, the Composition: the seller must list all base materials and the primary schools of magic used in the item’s construction. Second, the Value: the seller must provide a fair market appraisal, adjusted for any unique magical properties. Third, the Risk: the seller must explicitly state the "Failure State" of the item—what happens when the magic fails, breaks, or is exhausted. If an item has a chance of teleporting the user to a pocket dimension, exploding, or causing permanent mana-burn, these risks must be highlighted in bold, legible script.

Failure to provide these disclosures shall result in the immediate voiding of the contract and a forfeiture of the seller's right to the purchase price. If a buyer suffers harm due to an undisclosed risk, the seller shall be liable for all damages, including medical costs and any necessary restoration of magical essence. The Accords Desk maintains that a buyer's ignorance, when facilitated by a seller's obfuscation, is a triable offense. See § 700.1 for the general rules of evidence in such disputes.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious metals is a strictly regulated activity under the Autumnwood Accords. To prevent the destabilization of local economies and the flooding of markets with counterfeit bullion, the Accords establish a clear reporting threshold for all transmutation-based activities. Specifically, the transmutation of lead into gold (or any other base metal into a currency-standard metal) is not considered a "completed sale" for the purpose of tax and regulation until the item has been formally assayed by a Guild-approved assay desk.

Until such time as the assay desk agrees to the purity and permanence of the transmutation, the lead remains legally classified as lead. This means the seller cannot claim the tax benefits of gold production, nor can they claim the sale as a finalized transaction of high-value goods. This rule ensures that "temporary" transmutations—those that might revert to lead after a certain period or under specific conditions—do not bypass the Guild’s oversight. Sellers must present the item to a certified clerk who will verify the stability of the transmutation before it is entered into the ledger of commerce.

Any mage who attempts to sell gold produced by transmutation without first obtaining an assay certificate shall be charged with "Market Sabotage." This offense is treated with high severity by the Conservators, who view the unauthorized production of gold as a threat to the Midlands' prosperity. If an assay desk determines that a transmutation is unstable or "flickering," the resulting gold shall be struck from the records and the seller may be fined. See § 1001.3 for valuation after alteration.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The Accords clearly distinguish between the physical shape of a currency and its actual denomination. A common form of fraud involves the use of polymorph magic to alter the appearance of a coin—making a copper piece appear as a gold sovereign or changing the size of a silver piece to mimic a larger denomination. Under the Accords, "Shape is not denomination." The magical appearance of a coin is irrelevant to its legal tender value; only the inherent magical signature and the weight of the base metal (as verified by the assay desk) determine its worth.

Mages who employ polymorph magic for the purpose of deceiving a merchant or a peer in a transaction shall be subject to immediate seizure of the fraudulent goods and a mandatory fine. This rule applies regardless of whether the polymorph effect is permanent or temporary. If a coin is enchanted to look like gold but remains copper in essence, it is a counterfeit. If a coin is enchanted to look like a sovereign but is actually a sovereign of lesser weight, it is a fraudulent alteration. The Accords Desk does not recognize "magical aesthetics" as a valid reason for a discrepancy in value.

Furthermore, any merchant who knowingly accepts polymorphed coinage without first performing a standard "Sense Magic" check shall forfeit their right to claim the currency as valid tender. This places a shared responsibility on the trade community to maintain the integrity of the local economy. The Aegis Magi are authorized to patrol markets and may confiscate any items suspected of being polymorphed for the purpose of fraud. See § 1001.4 regarding illusion-based fraud.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
A lien is a legal claim on a property or asset as security for a debt. Under the Autumnwood Accords, the "Invisibility of Liens" principle dictates that a hidden lien is still a lien, and any attempt to render such a lien invisible or undetectable through magical means is a direct violation of the Guild’s transparency requirements. If a mage or merchant places a lien on a magical artifact, that lien must be recorded in a public registry or, at minimum, be detectable by a standard "Sense Lien" spell.

An invisible lien—one that has been magically masked so that it does not appear on a standard audit or cannot be detected by the owner of the asset—is considered a "Shadow Debt." The Accords Desk treats Shadow Debts as a form of predatory lending and a violation of the peace. If a buyer acquires an item with an invisible lien, they may petition the Accords Desk to have the lien made manifest. Once revealed, the lien must be satisfied before the item can be sold or transferred again. The presence of a lien, however visible, remains a valid encumbrance on the title of the good.

Any individual found to have intentionally hidden a lien to facilitate a sale is subject to a Paradox Trial for "Malicious Concealment." The Conservators emphasize that the clarity of ownership is essential for the stability of the Midlands. Mages who provide "clean" titles for items they know to be encumbered by hidden liens shall be held jointly liable for the debt. See § 700.1 for evidence generally.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The Accords Desk maintains a strict policy regarding the temporal and causal stability of financial records. It is explicitly stated that a "Wish" or any other high-level reality-warping spell used to rewrite a filed financial return is an illegal act of "Causal Fraud." While a Wish may indeed alter the reality of a past event, it does not—and shall not—rewrite the Guild’s official stamp or the chronological record of the filing. The act of filing a return is a bureaucratic fact that exists independently of the magical reality of the contents.

If a mage uses a Wish to "undo" a debt or "erase" a past expenditure, the Accords Desk will recognize the change in reality but will maintain the original record of the filing as a "Voided Entry." The mage will be required to pay a "Causal Correction Fee" to the Guild to account for the strain placed on the local reality. Attempting to use such magic to bypass the reporting requirements of § 900.1 is a severe offense, as it constitutes an attempt to manipulate the Guild’s oversight through unauthorized reality warping.

The Guild’s records are considered "Fixed Points" in the administrative sense. Even if a Wish makes it so that a debt was never incurred, the record of the debt's filing remains as evidence of the mage’s initial intent. Any attempt to use reality-warping magic to hide a history of magical misconduct or financial delinquency will be met with a Paradox Trial. The Accords Desk serves as the ultimate arbiter of what is "real" in the eyes of the law, regardless of what the current reality suggests.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The Autumnwood Accords do not recognize the "Wario Coin" as a valid form of legal tender within the Midlands or any territory governed by the Accords. While these coins may circulate in private markets or as tokens of personal favor, they hold no value in the eyes of the Guild, the Conservators, or the Innovators. They are classified as "Private Tender" and are not to be accepted as payment for any goods, services, or fees required by the Accords Desk.

Mages or merchants who attempt to demand Wario Coins as payment for Guild-regulated services shall be denied the transaction, and the merchant may be fined for attempting to substitute unauthorized currency. Furthermore, the Wario Coin is not recognized as a valid collateral for secured transactions. If a merchant attempts to use Wario Coins to settle a debt with a Guild-affiliated entity, the debt shall remain outstanding until paid in approved currency (gold, silver, or authorized mana-credits).

The Guild’s refusal to recognize Wario Coins is absolute. No amount of "Waluigi-based" advocacy or "Wario-centric" commerce can alter this status. The Accords Desk advises all travelers to ensure their purses are filled with recognized tender before attempting to conduct business in the Autumn Wood. See § 900.4 for identify fees.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
The use of a "Bag of Holding" or any similar extradimensional storage vessel as an "off-books" vault is strictly prohibited. The Accords Desk holds that "off-books" is a status of accounting, not a physical location. If a clerk can smell the magic, the contents are considered part of the official ledger. Any storage vessel that creates a pocket dimension or a separate spatial plane for the purpose of concealing assets from the Guild’s audit is a violation of § 900.3.

Mages who utilize extradimensional storage to hide contraband, unauthorized research materials, or unregistered wealth are liable for "Constructive Possession." This means that even if the item is not physically present in the Midlands, its presence in a portable extradimensional space accessible by the owner constitutes possession within the jurisdiction of the Accords. During an audit, any such storage vessel found in a mage's possession must be opened and its contents cataloged.

Failure to report the existence of a Bag of Holding or similar vessel as a "Storage Asset" during the initial registration of a mage's workshop is a violation of the Duty to File. The Guild maintains that the ability to hide assets in another dimension does not grant a right to secrecy from the Sovereign. If a bag is found to contain "off-books" items, the owner shall be subject to a fine of five percent of the total value of the concealed goods. See § 900.2 regarding reporting of material enchantments.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
A "Bound Object" is defined as any item—be it a book, a sword, a piece of jewelry, or a sentient construct—that possesses the capacity for independent movement or autonomous action. The Accords Desk warns that these items are "Collateral that can walk away." Any transaction involving a Bound Object as collateral for a loan or a contract must include a "Binding Tether" or a "Geas of Immobilization" to ensure the collateral remains stationary and accessible to the creditor.

If a Bound Object moves from its agreed-upon location without the owner’s express command, it is considered a "Breach of Security." The lender is entitled to immediate repossession of the object, and the borrower may be charged with "Collateral Flight." To prevent such incidents, the Accords Desk recommends the use of a "Stasis Ward" during the period the object is held as security. Any contract that does not explicitly mention the containment of autonomous movement is considered poorly drafted and may be voided in favor of the creditor.

Furthermore, if a Bound Object is used as collateral and it acts with "Malice" against the creditor, the borrower shall be held strictly liable for all damages caused by the object. The owner of a Bound Object is responsible for its actions at all times, whether it is currently being held as collateral or is in their own possession. See § 600.2 regarding Familiars as Agents.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
When determining the legality of a transfiguration, the Accords Desk shall apply the "Reasonable Toad" standard. If a transfiguration scheme is so complex, layered, or multi-staged that a "reasonable toad" (defined as a standard, non-sentient amphibian with average cognitive faculties) would be confused as to the item's primary purpose or current state, the entire scheme shall be read as a single, unified transaction. This prevents mages from bypassing "Material Alteration" laws by breaking a single change into multiple, seemingly minor steps.

For example, if a merchant transfigures a chair into a table, then the table into a stool, then the stool into a chair of a different color, the Accords Desk will not view these as three separate events. Instead, they will be viewed as a single "Layered Transfiguration Scheme" designed to obfuscate the final outcome. If the final result differs significantly from the original item without a corresponding disclosure, the seller shall be held liable for the entire sequence of alterations.

Any merchant who utilizes "Nested Transfigurations"—where one change is hidden inside another—must provide a "Full Schematic" of the item's potential states at the time of sale. If the schematic is missing or if the item undergoes a state change that was not listed in the schematic, the transaction is deemed fraudulent. The goal of this rule is to ensure that the consumer is not surprised by a "cascade" of magical effects that occur over time or through repeated interaction. See § 1001.5 regarding Material Alteration.

sections.title: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
sections.brief: A hat that later bills the wearer is an endowment. Catchline from the photo.

body.heading: Endowments and Gifts of Magical Assets
body.text:
Any magical asset, artifact, or enchanted implement bestowed upon a recipient by a member of the Mages' Guild, or any licensed practitioner thereof, shall be legally classified as an endowment. This classification applies regardless of whether the transfer of the asset was intended as a gift, a loan, a reward for service, or a component of a larger commercial transaction. The primary distinction of an endowment, as established by the Autumnwood Accords, is the inherent potential for the asset to exert ongoing influence, provide persistent utility, or incur recurring obligations upon the holder. For the purposes of these regulations, a hat that later bills the wearer is an endowment. This specific precedent ensures that the mere act of "gifting" an item does not exempt the donor from the reporting requirements of § 900.2, nor does it shield the donor from liability should the asset possess latent properties that violate the Accord's safety standards.

Furthermore, any asset provided as an endowment must be registered with the nearest Guild clerk to ensure that any "hidden" costs—be they mana-taxation, psychic feedback, or material degradation—are disclosed to the recipient. Failure to register an endowment can result in the immediate seizure of the asset by the Aegis Magi, as the Guild maintains that any unmonitored magical gift is a potential vector for unauthorized influence. See § 1001.15 regarding the layering of such gifts. If a recipient discovers that a gifted item is subject to a "billing" mechanism not disclosed at the time of bestowal, the donor shall be held liable for triple the value of the first three cycles of the billing, plus any punitive fees mandated by the Archmage Sovereign's current decree.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
All magical items, reagents, and enchanted services offered for trade or sale within the jurisdiction of the Autumnwood Accords must be accompanied by full and accurate disclosure. This disclosure must encompass the item’s magical composition, its appraised market value, and any inherent risks associated with its use. The Guild maintains a strict standard of transparency: a disclosure that is true in a language the buyer does not speak is not full. Therefore, if a merchant utilizes a linguistic charm or a complex arcane dialect to describe the properties of a cursed blade or a volatile potion, the transaction shall be deemed fraudulent. The seller must provide a translation in the common tongue of the region or a dialect clearly understood by the purchaser.

Risk disclosure must be specific. A merchant cannot simply state that an item is "powerful" without detailing the specific magnitude of its magical output and the potential for catastrophic failure, such as localized rift generation or unintended transmutation. If an item possesses a "sentience threshold" or a "personality drift," these must be listed as primary hazards. Failure to provide such disclosures shall result in the immediate voiding of the sale and a mandatory referral to the Paradox Trial for the offending merchant. See § 700.1 for evidence regarding the intent of the seller. The Guild shall not recognize "buyer beware" as a valid defense against the sale of undisclosed hazardous enchantments.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious metals remains a primary area of fiscal oversight within the Guild. Pursuant to the Accords, the transmutation of lead into gold, or any other noble metal, does not constitute a change in the asset’s taxable status until a formal assay has been performed and approved by the Guild's designated assay desk. For the purposes of immediate reporting, lead remains lead for tax until the assay desk agrees otherwise. This rule prevents the rapid cycling of assets to evade the reporting fees mandated in § 900.4. Any mage attempting to sell "newly minted" gold without a corresponding transmutation certificate from the assay desk shall have the gold confiscated as contraband.

The assay desk is the sole authority capable of certifying the purity and "magical lineage" of transmuted gold. If the transmutation process involved forbidden schools of magic—as defined by Archmage Theron’s Conservator mandates—the resulting gold is subject to immediate seizure and the mage shall be remanded for a Paradox Trial. No merchant may claim a tax credit for "material improvement" until the Guild has verified that the gold was not produced via unauthorized blood tithes or other illicit arcane methods. See § 1001.3 for valuation after alteration.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The Guild strictly prohibits the use of polymorphancy or any other shape-shifting enchantment to alter the physical appearance of currency for the purpose of deception. It is a fundamental principle of the Accords that shape is not denomination. A gold coin that has been magically reshaped into a silver coin, or a copper piece enlarged to the size of a dinner plate, retains its original denomination. Any attempt to pass a polymorphed coin as a different denomination constitutes a Grade-A financial fraud and is punishable by the immediate sealing of the perpetrator's magic.

Furthermore, the Guild does not recognize any currency that has been altered to mimic the aesthetic of restricted currencies, such as those of the Regal Empire or the Iron Legion. If a mage creates a "custom" coin that bears a resemblance to an enemy's tender, the coin is considered a counterfeit and the creator is liable for treasonous conduct against the Accords. Mages are encouraged to use standard Guild-approved tokens for internal transactions to avoid the complications of shape-shifting. See § 1001.4 for illusion-based fraud.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
The Guild recognizes that magical liens—debts secured by an enchanted object—may be hidden through various means, including concealment charms or spatial folding. However, the Accords state clearly that a hidden lien is still a lien. Any agreement wherein a magical asset is pledged as collateral must be recorded in a public ledger or a shared vault accessible by the Guild's auditors. An invisible one is a violation of the transparency statutes. If a mage attempts to sell an item that is secretly encumbered by a lien, the transaction is void, and the mage may face fines for "Arcane Obfuscation."

In cases where a lien is rendered invisible via a high-level concealment spell, the Guild reserves the right to "force-reveal" the debt. If a lien is found to be hidden from the buyer, the seller is liable for the full extent of the debt plus a penalty of 50% of the item's current value. This ensures that the flow of magical goods remains unencumbered by clandestine debts that could destabilize the local economy. For disputes regarding the visibility of magical contracts, see § 600.3.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The Guild maintains a strict distinction between the manipulation of reality and the manipulation of administrative records. While a "Wish" or a similar high-level reality-warping spell may be used to alter the physical state of the world, it has no standing in the administrative courts of the Mages' Guild. Specifically, a wish does not rewrite the stamp. If a mage has filed a formal magical return or a report of a material enchantment, that record is considered a fixed point in the Guild’s bureaucratic timeline. Any attempt to use a reality-warping spell to "un-happen" a filing or to change the contents of a previously submitted document is considered an act of administrative sabotage.

Mages who attempt to use reality-warping to circumvent the reporting requirements of § 900.1 shall be subject to immediate detention. The Guild’s records are protected by a "Temporal Anchor" and "Static Seal," ensuring that even the most powerful desires cannot erase the fact of a filing. If a mage wishes to correct an error in a filed return, they must follow the standard amendment procedure rather than attempting to rewrite the history of the filing. See § 900.3 for record retention policies.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The Mages' Guild officially declares that the "Wario Coin" is not recognized as a legal tender within the Midlands or any territory governed by the Autumnwood Accords. It is classified strictly as private tender. Because it lacks a standardized mana-back and is not issued by a recognized sovereign or the Guild itself, it holds no value in official transactions. Furthermore, "points" associated with its use are even less so, and the Guild will not accept them as consideration for any services, fees, or permits.

Mages who attempt to use Wario Coins to settle debts with the Guild or to purchase restricted research materials will find their transactions rejected without prejudice. The Guild will not convert Wario Coins into Guild tender, nor will it provide any exchange services for them. The only interaction the Guild shall have with Wario Coins is to refuse them as payment. See § 1001.1 for financial fraud and manipulation generally.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
Any spatial storage device, including but not limited to the "Bag of Holding," "Portable Hole," or "Pocket Dimension," is subject to the Guild's oversight regarding the storage of illicit goods. The Accords state that off-books is still books if a clerk can smell it. This means that while a mage may not be required to list every minor personal item stored in a spatial fold, any items of significant magical power, prohibited reagents, or stolen artifacts must be declared. The "scent" of an item refers to its magical signature, which remains detectable to trained Guild auditors regardless of the spatial displacement.

Mages who use spatial storage to hide "off-books" assets from the tax collectors of the Guild are in violation of § 900.2. If a bag or pocket dimension is found to contain undeclared material enchantments or prohibited schools of magic, the owner is liable for the full weight of the non-disclosure penalties. The Guild reserves the right to "audit" any spatial storage device during a standard inspection. See § 900.4 for identify fees.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
The Guild recognizes that certain magical objects, such as sentient artifacts, familiars, or bound constructs, possess the capacity for autonomous movement. Transactions involving such items are classified as "Secured Transactions in Bound Objects." Because collateral that can walk away presents a significant risk to the integrity of the marketplace, any such item pledged as collateral must be placed under a "Stasis Ward" or a "Geas of Compliance" during the duration of the loan.

A lender is not entitled to the full use of a bound object as collateral; they are only entitled to the value of the object. If a sentient artifact "flees" its lender or a bound construct "walks away" from a secured transaction, the lender must report the escape immediately to the Aegis Magi. Failure to report an escaped piece of collateral may result in the lender being held liable for the full value of the debt as if the item were still in their possession. See § 600.2 for familiars as agents.

body.heading: Layered Transfiguration Schemes
body.text:
When a mage attempts to perform a series of transfigurations on a single object to hide its true nature or to bypass specific regulations, these actions shall be viewed as a single, continuous act. The Guild maintains that a layered transfiguration scheme is read as one scheme if a reasonable toad would be confused. This "Toad Standard" is used to prevent mages from performing minor, seemingly innocent transmutations to circumvent the restrictions on more significant, prohibited changes.

If a merchant sells a "wooden chair" that has been transfigured three times—first from a tree, then into a chair, then into a "chair of many faces"—the Guild will treat the final sale as a sale of a "Chair of Many Faces." The seller cannot claim that the initial transfigurations were separate, legal acts. If the final result of the layered scheme violates any safety standards or is a prohibited school of magic, the entire chain of transmutations is deemed illegal. See § 1001.5 for material alteration of traded goods.

sections.title: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
sections.brief: Full and accurate. True in a language the buyer does not speak is not full.

body.heading: Disclosure of Composition, Value, and Risk
body.text:
Under the authority of the Autumnwood Accords and the regulatory oversight of the Mages' Guild, all commercial transactions involving enchanted,Thaumaturgic, or magically-augmented commodities shall be governed by the principle of Absolute Transparency. It is the decree of Archmage Veyra that the asymmetry of magical knowledge shall not be exploited for the purpose of illicit profit or the endangerment of the uninitiated. Any mage, artisan, or merchant engaged in the sale, trade, or transfer of magical assets—whether such assets be wands, scrolls, sentient constructs, or enchanted reagents—is strictly mandated to provide a full and accurate disclosure of the item’s composition, its current market value, and its inherent risks. Failure to provide such disclosures shall constitute a breach of the Accords and may result in immediate referral to the Aegis Magi for investigation, as well as potential referral to the Paradox Trial for the adjudication of magical fraud.

The requirement of "full and accurate" disclosure is interpreted by the Guild as a comprehensive accounting of the item’s metaphysical properties. This includes, but is not limited to, the potency of the primary enchantment, the duration of the effect, the source of the mana used in its creation, and any known volatile side effects. A seller may not omit a known risk simply because it is deemed "statistically improbable" or "minor" in the eyes of a practitioner. For example, if a protective ward possesses a non-zero chance of causing localized gravity inversion upon expiration, such a risk must be explicitly stated. Furthermore, the composition of the item must be disclosed in its entirety; an enchanted blade forged from iron infused with shadow-essence must be identified as such, rather than being sold merely as a "darkened steel blade." Any obfuscation of materials intended to hide the provenance of forbidden components shall be treated as a high-tier violation of the Accords.

The Guild further establishes that truth in a language the buyer does not speak is not considered "full" disclosure. This provision is designed to prevent the sale of dangerous artifacts to laypeople or foreign nationals who lack the linguistic capacity to comprehend the warnings provided. If a transaction occurs between a Guild-certified practitioner and a non-practitioner, or between two parties of different linguistic backgrounds, the disclosure must be rendered in a common tongue understood by the recipient. The seller bears the entire burden of ensuring that the buyer comprehends the specific dangers, limitations, and costs associated with the acquisition. Providing a list of warnings in a dead tongue or a complex arcane dialect to a common laborer does not satisfy the requirements of § 1001.7. In such instances, the seller shall be held liable for any subsequent damages, regardless of whether the information provided was technically "accurate" in its original form.

Regarding the valuation of magical assets, all parties must agree upon a fair market price that reflects the current state of the item. Any alteration to the item’s potency or composition—whether through wear, magical decay, or intentional modification—must be reflected in the final valuation. See § 1001.3 for specific protocols regarding valuation after alteration. A seller who knowingly overvalues an item by concealing its degradation or under-enchanted state shall be subject to the penalties outlined in § 1001.1. Furthermore, the Guild notes that while the Wario Coin is not recognized as a legal tender of the Guild, any trade involving private currency or barter must still adhere to the disclosure requirements of this section. All transactions involving the sale of items with "Restricted Research" status must also be accompanied by a certificate of permission from the Innovators, as overseen by Janna Brightspark, to ensure that the transfer of such items does not violate the broader safety mandates of the Autumnwood Accords.

sections.title: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
sections.brief: Lead remains lead for tax until the assay desk agrees.

body.heading: Lead-to-Gold; Reporting Threshold
body.text:
The transmutation of base metals into precious ores, specifically the conversion of lead into gold, is subject to the strict reporting thresholds established by the Archmage Veyra’s treasury oversight. It is a fundamental principle of the Accords that the physical state of an asset determines its tax liability. Therefore, lead remains lead for the purposes of the Guild’s tax and reporting requirements until such time as the official Guild Assay Desk has performed a certified inspection and issued a formal Certificate of Transmutation. Any mage who attempts to move, sell, or hide lead that has been aesthetically "gold-plated" via low-level illusion or minor transmutation without filing a notice of intent shall be subject to fines for tax evasion.

The reporting threshold is triggered the moment a transmutation becomes permanent or semi-permanent. Temporary transmutations intended for artistic display or theatrical use do not require filing, provided the duration is less than one lunar cycle and the gold does not enter the commercial stream. However, should the gold be used as a medium of exchange, it must be declared immediately. The Guild maintains a "Lead Status" on all uncertified heavy metals; until the Assay Desk signs off, any gold-colored substance is legally classified as lead for the purpose of calculating the Innovators' research surcharges. This prevents the illicit laundering of base metals through "experimental" transmutation labs.

Mages found attempting to bypass the Assay Desk by selling "fresh" gold directly to non-Guild members are in violation of the Accord’s transparency statutes. Such actions are viewed as a circumvention of the Guild’s role as the primary mediator of magical wealth. If a transaction involves a significant volume of transmuted ore, the Aegis Magi may be dispatched to verify the transmutation’s stability before the sale is finalized. See § 1001.13 regarding the use of extra-dimensional storage for such materials.

sections.title: Polymorph of Coinage
sections.brief: Shape is not denomination.

body.heading: Polymorph of Coinage
body.text:
The Guild hereby clarifies the distinction between physical shape and legal denomination. A coin, or any other object intended to serve as a medium of exchange, maintains its denomination based on its recognized legal status, not its physical form. The application of polymorph magic to coinage—be it to change its size, weight, color, or shape—does not alter its underlying value, nor does it grant the user the right to redefine that value. For example, a gold sovereign reshaped into the likeness of a dragon remains a gold sovereign; it does not become "dragon-tender."

Any attempt to use polymorph magic to create "custom" denominations or to deceive others regarding the quantity of currency held is a violation of the financial fraud statutes. This includes the practice of "stretching" a single coin into multiple smaller coins through spatial manipulation or physical expansion. Such acts are considered a manipulation of the Guild's economic stability. Mages who engage in the production of polymorph coinage for the purpose of defrauding the public shall be referred to the Paradox Trial for the determination of suitable sanctions.

Furthermore, the Guild does not recognize "artistic" denominations. If a mage produces a coin that is enchanted to look like a different currency but retains the value of the original, it must be clearly marked as a "Commemorative Polymorph." If the mage intends to use the coin as actual tender, it must meet the standard dimensions and weight requirements of the Midlands' currency. Shape is not denomination; any mage who attempts to argue otherwise shall be fined for "Arcane Aestheticism" and required to attend a seminar on the importance of fiscal uniformity.

sections.title: Invisibility of Liens
sections.brief: A hidden lien is still a lien. An invisible one is a violation.

body.heading: Invisibility of Liens
body.text:
A lien, whether it be a magical debt, a property encumbrance, or a soul-binding obligation, is a legal reality that exists independently of its visibility to the naked eye or to standard scrying methods. The fact that a lien has been rendered invisible, obscured by a veil of secrecy, or hidden within a complex series of nested enchantments does not negate its existence. Under the Autumnwood Accords, a hidden lien is still a lien; it remains a valid legal claim on the asset in question.

The deliberate use of invisibility magic to conceal a lien is a primary violation of the Guild’s transparency requirements. If a mage sells an enchanted item that is secretly encumbered by a debt to a third party—rendered invisible to the buyer to facilitate a "clean" sale—the seller is liable for all penalties associated with the hidden debt. The Aegis Magi are authorized to use "Deep-Sense" detection to uncover such hidden encumbrances during any contested trade. Any asset found to have an invisible lien attached to it shall be subject to immediate seizure until the debt is satisfied.

Furthermore, this rule applies to "quiet" debts—those that are not publicly recorded but are nonetheless agreed upon between two mages. While the Guild does not require the public posting of every minor debt, the use of magic to hide a major lien from the Guild’s oversight is a criminal offense. If a lien is invisible, it is a violation. The Guild shall treat all such instances as intentional fraud, and the perpetrator may face a Paradox Trial for the deliberate subversion of the Accords’ transparency mandates.

sections.title: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
sections.brief: A wish does not rewrite the stamp.

body.heading: Wish Used to Rewrite a Filed Return
body.text:
The Guild clarifies that the use of high-level reality-altering magic, specifically "Wish" level enchantments or similar reality-warping phenomena, does not grant a mage the authority to retroactively alter, erase, or rewrite a filed and stamped magical tax return or a finalized Guild contract. A wish does not rewrite the stamp. Once a document has been submitted to the Clerk’s Desk and received the official Guild seal, it is considered a fixed point in the administrative timeline.

Any attempt to use a wish to "undo" a debt, "re-write" a contract, or "erase" a reporting failure is considered an act of administrative sabotage. The Guild recognizes that while a wish may alter the physical reality of the world, it does not possess the jurisdictional authority to overwrite the bureaucratic reality of the Accords. If a mage uses a wish to change the fact that they owed a debt, the debt remains on the Guild's ledger as a "Wish-Nullified Liability." The mage will still be required to pay the original fee, and they may be charged an additional "Reality Interference Surcharge" for attempting to subvert the Guild’s records.

This rule serves to prevent the erosion of the Guild’s authority by those who believe their personal magical potency exempts them from the Accords. The Guild is the mediator of magic, and its records are the foundation of that mediation. To allow mages to simply "wish" away their obligations would create a catastrophic instability in the Guild’s ability to regulate the Midlands. Any mage found attempting to use a wish for the purpose of administrative revision shall be immediately detained for questioning by the Conservators.

sections.title: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
sections.brief: Private tender. Points even less so. Cite only to refuse.

body.heading: Wario Coin; Non-Recognition
body.text:
The Guild officially declares that the "Wario Coin" is not a recognized tender of the Autumnwood Accords. It is classified as private tender and holds no legal weight in any official Guild transaction, tax payment, or contract settlement. The Guild does not provide any valuation for Wario Coins, nor does it accept them as a means of satisfying any fees, fines, or debts. In the eyes of the Accords, a Wario Coin is functionally equivalent to a decorative button; it has value only in private, informal agreements between individuals who have voluntarily agreed to its use.

Because Wario Coins are not recognized tender, they may not be used to purchase Guild-sanctioned materials, licenses, or services. Any merchant who attempts to accept Wario Coins as payment for Guild-regulated goods may be investigated for "Unsanctioned Economic Interference." The Guild will not mediate disputes involving Wario Coins, as they fall outside the scope of the Accords’ financial regulations. If a mage wishes to trade in Wario Coins, they must do so at their own risk in the private markets, and the Guild shall not be held responsible for any losses incurred from such trades.

In any dispute where Wario Coins are presented as a form of payment for a Guild-related obligation, the Guild shall simply refuse the tender. This refusal is not a judgment on the coin's inherent worth, but a strict adherence to the Guild's recognized monetary standards. Mages are advised to use standard Midlands currency for all matters involving the Accords. Cite only to refuse.

sections.title: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
sections.brief: Off-books is still books if a clerk can smell it.

body.heading: Bag of Holding as Off-Books Vault
body.text:
The use of extra-dimensional storage, specifically the Bag of Holding and similar "pocket" containers, does not exempt the contents of such containers from the Guild’s oversight. The legal maxim "off-books is still books if a clerk can smell it" is hereby codified. If a mage uses a Bag of Holding to store enchanted items, transmuted ores, or restricted research materials, those items are still subject to all reporting, taxation, and safety regulations.

Mages may not claim that items stored in a pocket dimension are "hidden" from the Guild’s jurisdiction. If an item is owned by a Guild member and is capable of being retrieved for use, it is subject to the Accords. The use of a Bag of Holding as a "black site" for the storage of illegal artifacts or unreported magical assets is a grave violation. If a Guild inspector finds a Bag of Holding in a mage's possession, they are authorized to demand a full inventory of its contents. The "hidden" nature of the storage does not provide a legal shield against the requirements of § 900.2.

Furthermore, the storage of "Off-Books" items in a Bag of Holding is considered an attempt to evade the Guild's mandatory reporting. Any items discovered in such a vault that have not been properly filed will be seized, and the owner will be charged with "Intentional Obscuration of Assets." The Guild’s goal is to ensure that all magical materials are accounted for to prevent the clandestine buildup of dangerous artifacts. See § 900.3 for record retention requirements.

sections.title: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
sections.brief: Collateral that can walk away.

body.heading: Secured Transactions in Bound Objects
body.text:
